name: Marrakech
tagline: The 17th-century palace where Hitchcock filmed a scene, and the square that fills with 40 food stalls each night.

Dar Essalam.description: A 17th-century palace turned into the city's first Moroccan restaurant, since 1952. Alfred Hitchcock filmed "The Man Who Knew Too Much" here in 1956.

La Mamounia.description: Formal Moroccan cuisine at one of the world's most legendary hotels, with gold-leaf pastilla.

Jemaa el-Fnaa.description: The UNESCO World Heritage square that turns into Morocco's biggest street food market by night, with nearly 40 stalls.

Al Fassia Guéliz.description: A restaurant run entirely by women since 1985, traditional Fez cuisine and a regular on The World's 50 Best Discovery.

Nomad.description: Modern Moroccan cuisine on a four-story rooftop over the Rahba Kedima spice square, with views of the Atlas.

Dar Moha.description: An 18th-century riad once home to designer Pierre Balmain, now the restaurant of chef Moha Fedal, pioneer of "new Moroccan cuisine." Dinners are served beside a pool decorated with Berber-inspired mosaics.

Le Tobsil.description: A restaurant set in a medina riad, known for candlelit dinners with rose petals scattered on the tables and live Gnawa music.

Dar Yacout.description: A medina palace turned dining landmark for more than three decades, with a rooftop terrace overlooking the Koutoubia and the Atlas Mountains.

La Maison Arabe.description: Founded in 1946 by Hélène and Suzy Sébillon-Larochette, it was the medina's first restaurant open to foreigners and hosted guests like Churchill and Hemingway. It is now home to Morocco's first cooking school, opened in 2001.

Le Foundouk.description: A rooftop restaurant in a historic medina building, serving Moroccan and international cuisine; closed on Wednesdays.

Café de France.description: A terrace café founded in 1912 facing Jemaa el-Fnaa square, a historic meeting spot for Europeans since the French Protectorate, with views of the Koutoubia.

Chez Chegrouni.description: A no-frills spot beside Jemaa el-Fnaa where orders are scribbled on paper napkins; famous for its rooftop terrace overlooking the square at sunset.

Grand Café de la Poste.description: A former 1925 post office, the first building in the Guéliz district, converted into a colonial-style brasserie that was once a meeting spot for painter Jacques Majorelle.

Kosybar.description: A multi-level bar on Place des Ferblantiers in the Kasbah, with a rooftop terrace looking out over sunset views above the Bahia Palace.

Le Barométre.description: A speakeasy cocktail bar opened in 2016 by the Hadni brothers, Morocco's first bar built entirely around mixology, hidden behind an unmarked door in Guéliz.

Sky Bar.description: A rooftop bar atop Hotel La Renaissance at Guéliz's central junction, with a 360-degree panorama taking in the Atlas Mountains, the Koutoubia and the new city.

Café des Épices.description: A café on the Rahba Kedima spice square since 2000, with a multi-level terrace overlooking the bustle of the souk below.

Terrasse des Épices.description: A restaurant on the rooftop of Souk Cherifia since 2007, with tables set among plants overlooking the medina's rooftops.

Dar Cherifa.description: A late-16th-century Saadian house, one of the oldest and best-preserved in the medina; restored in 2000, it now operates as a literary café and art gallery.

Nid'Cigogne.description: A restaurant facing the Saadian Tombs whose name means "stork's nest," after the storks nesting on the neighboring rooftop; a three-level terrace recommended by Frommer's.

Maison de la Photographie.description: A museum founded in 2009 by Patrick Menac'h and Hamid Mergani, holding a collection of over 4,500 photographs of Morocco taken between 1870 and 1950; its rooftop houses one of the medina's best-view cafés.

Pâtisserie Al Jawda.description: A Guéliz pastry shop beloved by locals for its Moroccan and French sweets, especially its macarons and gazelle horn cookies.

Bacha Coffee.description: A coffee house founded in 1910 in the Dar el Bacha Palace, once frequented by Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Josephine Baker; revived in 2017 inside the palace-turned-museum.

Café Arabe.description: A restaurant on Rue Mouassine blending Italian and Moroccan cuisine, with a panoramic rooftop over the medina's rooftops.

Naranj.description: A family-run Lebanese restaurant on Riad Zitoun el Jdid, with vegetarian options and traditional mezze.

Plus61.description: An Australian-owned bistro in Guéliz that makes its own bread, pasta, cheese and yogurt daily, with a kitchen blending Mediterranean and Australian influences.

Amal Center.description: A nonprofit social-gastronomy restaurant founded in 2012 by Nora Belahcen Fitzgerald, where disadvantaged women train in Moroccan cooking over several months; lunch only, with a menu that changes daily, in Guéliz.

Chez Lamine Hadj Mustapha.description: An institution since 1965 in Mechoui Alley, just off Jemaa el-Fnaa; up to 40 whole lambs are slow-roasted each morning in underground wood-fired ovens.

Marché Central Guéliz.description: The new town's covered food market, relocated to Rue Ibn Toumert after the Carré Eden mall took over its original 1920s site; stalls sell fresh seafood, cheese and organic produce.

La Cantine des Gazelles.description: A family-style restaurant near Jemaa el-Fnaa specializing in home-style Moroccan cooking: couscous, kefta, tagines and pastillas.

Café Clock Marrakech.description: A cultural café in the Kasbah, sister to the original in Fez, famous for its camel burger and traditional storytelling nights.

Comptoir Darna.description: The dinner-cabaret that pioneered the format in Marrakech in 1999, set in a 1930s Art Deco villa in Hivernage, with live belly dancing and a Gnaoua orchestra.

Earth Café.description: A pioneer of vegan and vegetarian cooking in the medina since 2007, serving dishes made with organic ingredients.

La Trattoria Marrakech.description: Marrakech's longest-running Italian restaurant, open since 1974 in a Guéliz Art Deco villa designed by decorator Bill Willis.

Le Jardin.description: A restaurant set in a 16th-century medina building, with a lush garden courtyard and modern Moroccan cooking using local ingredients.

Mizaan.description: A restaurant opened in 2024 on Avenue Mohammed V in Guéliz, with rope sculpture around the bar and reinvented Moroccan cooking; featured in Time Out Marrakech's restaurant picks.

El Fenn.description: A riad-hotel opened in 2004 by Vanessa Branson, sister of Richard Branson, with a restaurant and rooftop bar; it has appeared on Condé Nast Traveler's Gold List in 2017, 2021, 2022 and 2024.

Kechmara.description: A Guéliz fixture since 2004: a café, bar and bistro with a seventies design sensibility, a leafy rooftop terrace and live music on Thursdays and Fridays.

Patisserie des Princes.description: A historic pastry shop steps from Jemaa el-Fnaa, a medina institution for traditional Moroccan sweets.

Le Tanjia.description: A three-floor restaurant in the Mellah, near the Badii and Bahia palaces, with a central courtyard, panoramic rooftop and live music and belly-dancing shows.
